Chapter 1: Laying the Foundation—Morality Beyond Experience
When you think about what’s right and wrong, where do you usually start? Most of us look to our own feelings, the things people around us expect, or maybe just what seems to make everyone happy. But if we’re after a moral philosophy that works for everyone—no matter where or when—they’re just not enough.
To build a foundation that really holds up, we need something sturdier than changing customs or shifting moods. We’ve got to ground morality in reason itself—something that stands apart from the unpredictable world of experience.
Picture a compass that always points north. No matter where you are, or what’s going on around you, you can count on it to be steady and true. That’s what the principles of morality should be like too—constant and unchanging, untouched by personal wishes or cultural swings.
Philosophers call this approach a metaphysics of morals. Instead of searching for right and wrong in the messy world of habits and happiness, it asks us to look to pure reason—the one thing that doesn’t bend to trends or personal taste.
Now, think about the reasons people give for helping someone out. Maybe it just feels good. Maybe you hope they’ll return the favor someday. Or maybe it’s just what everyone around you does. But if we’re trying to find what makes an action truly moral, these kinds of reasons don’t quite get us there. They’re tied to feelings, outcomes, or social routines—all things that can change from one moment to the next.
Here’s something to pay attention to: morality can’t just be a collection of handy rules or a clever way to make people happy. It needs to be a set of principles that work for anyone, anywhere—no matter who they are or what they want. And the only way to get there is by rooting it in reason itself. The same kind of reason that gives us math and logic—truths that don’t change just because someone wishes they would.
This brings us to a really important distinction. There’s empirical knowledge—what we pick up from experience, the things we see, touch, or learn from the world around us. And then there’s a priori knowledge—truths we arrive at through reason alone, with no need to check the facts outside ourselves.
If we want morality to be universal, it has to be grounded in these a priori principles. Just like arithmetic doesn’t depend on how we feel about numbers, right and wrong shouldn’t depend on what people happen to want, or what makes them feel good in the moment.
So, that’s where our journey begins—searching for the basic laws of morality that reason alone can uncover. Laws that can guide anyone, anywhere, toward what’s right, no matter what the world throws at us.
